columns/many: Say you have one matrix, A, two by three, and four vectors of three numbers each, all to go through it.
columns/one: One at a time, that is four matrix-vector products, and each one turns three numbers into two.
columns/stand: Stand the four vectors side by side, and they make a single matrix, B: three rows, and four columns, one per vector.
columns/AB: Multiplying A by B, written A B, does all four at once. A times each column of B gives the same column of the result.
columns/shape: Four answers of two numbers each: the result is two by four.
columns/fit: Each column of B goes into A, so it must be as long as a row of A. A's columns must equal B's rows: here, three and three.
columns/inner: Written as shapes, two by three, times three by four, the threes sit in the middle: they are the inner dimensions.
columns/outer: The result keeps the outer ones: two rows from A, and four columns from B.
columns/m: For any sizes, call A's rows m.
columns/n: Call the inner dimension, where A and B meet, n.
columns/rule: Then m by n, times n by k, gives m by k. The two inner sizes, both n, must match, and they vanish from the result.
chain/turn: Here is a second way to see it. A matrix turns one vector into another: B, three by four, turns four numbers into three.
chain/then: Then A, two by three, turns those three into two.
chain/handoff: The hand-off is the rule: what B gives out must be as long as what A takes in. B's rows must equal A's columns.
chain/cayley: That is how Arthur Cayley defined the product of two matrices, in eighteen fifty eight, in his Memoir on the Theory of Matrices: one applied after the other, combined into a single matrix.
chain/rect: He gave the shape rule too: the second matrix needs as many rows as the first has columns.
chain/once: So A B, two by four, does both steps at once: four numbers straight to two. The three in the middle is used up inside, which is why the inner dimension vanishes.
chain/C: A longer chain works the same way. Put a third matrix, C, four by five, on the right: it turns five numbers into the four that B takes.
chain/ABC: Combine two at a time: A B is two by four, and two by four, times four by five, gives two by five.
order/swap: Order matters. Swap them, B times A, and a row of B has four numbers, while a column of A has only two. Nothing pairs up, so there is no product.
order/M: Now take A and a new matrix, M, two by four. A times M fails too: A's rows have three numbers, and M's columns have two.
order/T: Transpose A, turning its rows into columns: A transpose is three by two.
order/fix: Now its rows have two numbers, like M's columns. Three by two, times two by four, gives three by four.
order/flip: M transpose times A works too, but gives four by three. The rows come from the first matrix and the columns from the second, so the order sets the shape.
